prompt.context: It is early 2003 and you are staffed at a leading ISP. It has been a dismal year with declining profits for this company and the CEO has recently announced that this will be a reset year and that they are looking forward to 2004 being a rebound year with aggressive revenue growth. The CEO has been getting mixed messages from 3 camps within the organization. One camp thinks AOL should focus only on content and ditch the dial-up service offering. Another thinks they should focus on connectivity alone, and a third camp thinks that the best strategy to grow revenues in 2004 is to focus on both.
prompt.question: We have been asked by the CEO to recommend some actions. We are in the first team meeting — what issues do you think we should look at to assess the situation and come up with a recommendation?

clarifying_info.q: What specific products and services does the client provide?
clarifying_info.a: The client offers connectivity through a dial-up service only, and provides content to its customers.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client develop all of its own content, or does it partner with others?
clarifying_info.a: They develop content as well as partner with others to provide content.

clarifying_info.q: Has there been significant price decline in the past year?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the competition in the dial-up space has been fierce and has been driving prices down. The client currently charges on average $20/month for its service.

clarifying_info.q: Has the client been losing a significant number of customers?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, they currently have 27 million customers, but in 2003 so far 17 million have left.

clarifying_info.q: Can you tell me more about the segmentation and value drivers of the client's customers?
clarifying_info.a: Customers can be separated broadly by age: under 20 are driven by price and looking for cheap connectivity; 20-45 have wider bandwidth needs; over 45 value convenience and simplicity.

clarifying_info.q: Has the client thought about developing a broadband product offering?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Two options are currently being considered: (1) partner with a local DSL/Cable service provider to offer their service with a broadband version of the content; (2) our client chooses the right connection (DSL or Cable) for its customers based on what is available in their area.

clarifying_info.q: How long does it take to develop new content internally?
clarifying_info.a: New content takes 6-12 months to create internally.

framework: Understand the client's current revenue model: connectivity (dial-up) vs. content offerings
Diagnose the profit decline: pricing pressure from dial-up competition and customer churn
Analyze customer segmentation by age/value driver to identify which segments are churning and why
Evaluate the broadband opportunity: build vs. partner, cost structure, revenue upside from churn reduction and new customer acquisition
Identify quick-win revenue generation options for 2004 given the 6-12 month content development lead time
Synthesize a recommendation for the CEO on whether to focus on content, connectivity, or both

questions.prompt: What is driving the profit decline?
questions.guidance: Two interrelated drivers: (1) revenue pressure from dial-up price competition — client charges $20/month but prices are being pushed down; (2) massive customer churn — 17 million of the customer base have left in 2003, leaving only 27 million remaining. Together these compress both price realization and subscriber volume.

questions.prompt: Which customer segment is most at risk and why?
questions.guidance: The 20-45 age group has wider bandwidth needs and is the most likely segment churning to broadband (DSL/Cable) providers. The under-20 group is price-sensitive and may still use dial-up for cost reasons. The over-45 group values convenience and simplicity and may be stickier on dial-up. Focusing retention efforts on the 20-45 segment is the highest-leverage action.

questions.prompt: What costs need to be considered to offer a broadband product?
questions.guidance: Four cost buckets: (1) Technology — building or leasing new infrastructure, partnership fees; (2) Content Development — creating broadband-optimized content; (3) Advertising — attracting new customers and retaining current ones; (4) Additional Overhead — customer service staffing and training costs.

questions.prompt: Between the two broadband options, which should the client choose?
questions.guidance: Option 1: partner with a local DSL/Cable provider and bundle broadband + content. Option 2: client selects the right connection for each customer based on local availability. The client should choose the option that gives the most control over costs and quality. Selecting the connection for customers (Option 2) provides greater cost control and allows the client to optimize the offer by geography, though it is more operationally complex.

questions.prompt: What quick revenue generation ideas can you suggest for 2004, given that new content takes 6-12 months to develop?
questions.guidance: Because organic content development has a 6-12 month lead time, the focus should be on partnerships and licensing. Ideas include: online music (partner with music providers); news and traditional TV programming delivered via the web; children's educational games (e.g., partner with Leap Frog to sell/download educational content); e-commerce or advertising revenue from the existing 27 million subscriber base; premium service tiers for the over-45 convenience-focused segment.

brainstorming.prompt: What products and services could the client quickly launch or partner on to generate revenue in 2004?

categories.name: Entertainment
ideas: Online music streaming or download partnerships
News delivery and traditional TV programming via the web
On-demand video content through broadband partners

categories.name: Education
ideas: Children's educational games (e.g., partner with Leap Frog for downloadable games)
Online tutoring or test-prep content partnerships
Adult continuing education or e-learning modules

categories.name: Broadband Connectivity Partnerships
ideas: Bundle broadband access with existing content subscription
Negotiate revenue-share deals with DSL/Cable providers
White-label broadband service targeting existing subscriber base

categories.name: Advertising and E-commerce
ideas: Sell targeted advertising to the 27 million subscriber base
Affiliate commerce tied to content (e.g., music purchases, game downloads)

categories.name: Premium Tiers
ideas: Premium simplicity/convenience package for over-45 segment
Business productivity tools for the 20-45 segment

recommendation: Focus on the 20-45 age segment where the majority of churn is occurring, driven by bandwidth limitations of dial-up
Partner with broadband (DSL/Cable) providers to offer a bundled broadband + content product, as this is faster to market than building own infrastructure
Simultaneously pursue quick-win revenue partnerships in entertainment and education to meet the 2004 revenue growth target without waiting for internally developed content
risks: Partnership dependence: relying on DSL/Cable partners reduces control over quality and pricing
Content commoditization: if competitors license the same content, the content advantage erodes
Speed of execution: 6-12 month content lead times mean 2004 revenue must come primarily from partnerships, which take time to negotiate
Customer retention is not guaranteed even with broadband offering if pricing remains uncompetitive
next_steps: Quantify the addressable revenue opportunity from stopping churn in the 20-45 segment
Identify and shortlist DSL/Cable partnership candidates in top geographic markets
Run a cost-benefit analysis on build vs. partner for broadband infrastructure
Develop a partnership pipeline for entertainment and education content to hit 2004 revenue targets
